clinicalPearls: Idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy is defined by restrictive ventricular physiology with impaired filling and raised filling pressures, near-normal wall thickness and normal or only mildly reduced systolic function, in the absence of an identifiable infiltrative, storage or endomyocardial cause.
Biatrial enlargement that is often marked, in the setting of non-dilated and non-hypertrophied ventricles, is a characteristic morphological signature.
Predominant right-sided congestion with elevated jugular venous pressure, ascites and oedema frequently dominates the clinical picture and can be mistaken for hepatic or renal disease.

The most important and difficult distinction is from constrictive pericarditis, because the latter is surgically curable; ventricular interdependence, respiratory variation in filling and pericardial features must be sought.
It is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion, so amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, Fabry disease and endomyocardial disease must be actively ruled out before the label is applied.

A subset is familial, associated with sarcomeric gene mutations (including troponin I) and may overlap phenotypically with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, warranting family screening and genetic counselling.
Atrial fibrillation and thromboembolism are common owing to atrial dilatation and stasis, and contribute substantially to morbidity.
Management is largely supportive, with cautious diuresis to relieve congestion while avoiding excessive preload reduction that compromises the already limited stroke volume.
reference.pathophysiology: The ventricular myocardium becomes abnormally stiff and non-compliant, so that even small increases in volume produce large increases in ventricular pressure. Systolic contraction and ventricular cavity size are relatively preserved, but impaired diastolic relaxation and compliance raise atrial and venous pressures, driving pulmonary and systemic congestion. Chronically elevated atrial pressures cause progressive biatrial dilatation while the ventricles remain non-dilated and of near-normal thickness. In familial disease, sarcomeric protein mutations alter myofilament function and calcium handling; in sporadic disease, variable interstitial fibrosis and myocyte disarray contribute to the stiff-ventricle physiology. The fixed limitation of ventricular filling ultimately caps cardiac output and, over time, may be accompanied by pulmonary hypertension and low-output heart failure.
additionalInvestigations: echocardiography with Doppler and tissue Doppler for restrictive filling and biatrial enlargement
cardiac magnetic resonance with tissue characterisation to exclude infiltration and pericardial disease
simultaneous or careful right and left heart catheterisation to distinguish restriction from constriction
serum free light chains and amyloid work-up including consideration of endomyocardial biopsy
genetic testing and family screening where familial disease is suspected
natriuretic peptides for severity and follow-up
cross-sectional imaging (CT) for pericardial thickening or calcification
redFlags: syncope or presyncope suggesting arrhythmia or critically limited output
refractory right heart failure with progressive ascites and cachexia
features suggesting a treatable mimic such as constrictive pericarditis or amyloidosis
rising filling pressures with worsening functional class despite therapy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable but often unfavourable once symptomatic heart failure develops, with progression to low-output failure and a significant risk of thromboembolism and arrhythmia; selected patients, particularly children and those with progressive disease, are considered for cardiac transplantation.
pitfalls: failing to exclude surgically curable constrictive pericarditis before labelling disease idiopathic
applying the diagnosis without excluding infiltrative and storage causes
over-diuresis that precipitates a fall in cardiac output and renal impairment
missing familial disease and the opportunity for family screening
underestimating thromboembolic risk in dilated, fibrillating atria
